claim: Bilaterian animals comprise more than 95% of the extant animals on earth.
source: Bilaterian animals comprise more than the 95% of the extant animals on earth and exhibit enormous body plan diversity (Martindale and Lee, 2013).
evidence: This is a cited factual statement about the proportion of bilaterian animals among extant animals.

claim: The emergence of mesoderm contributed to the explosion of biological diversity throughout evolution.
source: The emergence of mesoderm clearly contributed to the explosion of biological diversity throughout evolution (Martindale and Lee, 2013; Martindale, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Cnidarians are the sister group to bilaterians.
source: Cnidarians (e.g. sea anemones, corals, hydroids, and 'jellyfish') are the sister group to bilaterians, and despite their surprisingly complex genomes (Putnam et al., 2007), do not possess a distinct mesodermal tissue layer.
evidence: This is a cited statement about phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Cnidarians do not possess a distinct mesodermal tissue layer.
source: Cnidarians (e.g. sea anemones, corals, hydroids, and 'jellyfish') are the sister group to bilaterians, and despite their surprisingly complex genomes (Putnam et al., 2007), do not possess a distinct mesodermal tissue layer.
evidence: This is a cited statement about cnidarian anatomy.

claim: The gastrodermal lining of the cnidarian gut cavity consists of a bifunctional endomesodermal epithelium with molecular characteristics of both bilaterian endodermal and myoepithelial mesodermal cells.
source: Instead, the gastrodermal lining to their gut cavity consists of a bifunctional endomesodermal epithelium with molecular characteristics of both bilaterian endodermal and myoepithelial mesodermal cells (Martindale and Lee, 2013; Technau and Scholz, 2003; Martindale et al., 2004; Jahnel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Brachyury and snail genes contribute to the specification of endomesodermal fates in both bilaterian and cnidarian embryos.
source: For example, brachyury and snail, among other genes, contribute to the specification of the endomesodermal fates in both bilaterian and cnidarian embryos (Technau and Scholz, 2003; Martindale et al., 2004; Magie et al., 2007; Yasuoka et al., 2016; Servetnick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In bilaterians, mesodermal cells segregate from an embryonic endomesodermal precursor to form both endoderm and a third tissue layer (mesoderm) not present in the embryos of diploblastic cnidarians.
source: Yet in bilaterians, mesodermal cells segregate from an embryonic endomesodermal precursor to form both endoderm and a third tissue layer (mesoderm) not present in the embryos of diploblastic cnidarians (Martindale et al., 2004; Rodaway and Patient, 2001; Davidson et al., 2002; Maduro and Rothman, 2002; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Virtually all of the genes required for mesoderm formation are present in cnidarian genomes.
source: How mesodermal cells originally segregated from an ancestral endomesodermal epithelium during animal evolution is still unclear (Martindale and Lee, 2013; Martindale, 2005; Technau and Scholz, 2003), particularly because virtually all of the genes required for mesoderm formation are present in cnidarian genomes (Putnam et al., 2007; Baumgarten et al., 2015; Chapman et al., 2010; Shinzato et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies.

claim: In most bilaterian embryos, maternal determinants induce the localization of nuclear ß-catenin to blastomeres derived from the vegetal pole.
source: In most bilaterian embryos described to date, after a series of synchronous and stereotyped cleavage divisions, maternal determinants induce the localization of nuclear ß-catenin to blastomeres derived from the vegetal pole (Martindale and Lee, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Gastrulation and the specification of endomesodermal fates is restricted to the vegetal pole in most bilaterian embryos.
source: Hence, gastrulation and the specification of endomesodermal fates is restricted to the vegetal pole.
evidence: This is a statement following from the previous claim about nuclear ß-catenin localization.

claim: In bilaterians, brachyury is expressed at the border of the blastopore and snail is expressed in the prospective mesodermal tissues.
source: In these species, brachyury is expressed at the border of the blastopore and snail is expressed in the prospective mesodermal tissues (Technau and Scholz, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The formation of mesoderm involves the downregulation of E-cadherin, loss of apicobasal cell polarity, and in some cases, the induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: The formation of mesoderm involves a variety of cellular processes including the downregulation of E-cadherin, loss of apicobasal cell polarity, and in some cases, the induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012; Schäfer et al., 2014; Acloque et al., 2009; Lim and Thiery, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Embryos of Nematostella vectensis develop without a stereotyped cleavage pattern but cell fates become organized along the embryonic animal-vegetal axis.
source: Embryos of the cnidarian starlet sea anemone N. vectensis develop without a stereotyped cleavage pattern but cell fates become organized along the embryonic animal-vegetal axis (Fritzenwanker et al., 2007; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: During blastula formation in N. vectensis, embryonic cells form a single hollow epithelial layer.
source: During blastula formation, embryonic cells of N. vectensis form a single hollow epithelial layer.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about N. vectensis development.

claim: Epithelial cells of the animal pole in N. vectensis, characterized by the nuclear localization of Nvß-catenin prior to gastrulation, invaginate by apical constriction to form the endomesodermal epithelium.
source: Epithelial cells of the animal pole, characterized by the nuclear localization of Nvß-catenin prior to gastrulation (Wikramanayake et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007), invaginate by apical constriction to form the endomesodermal epithelium (Magie et al., 2007; Tamulonis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The expression of Nvbrachyury around the presumptive border of the blastopore and Nvsnail genes in the presumptive endomesodermal gastrodermis of N. vectensis embryos occurs even before the morphological process of gastrulation begins.
source: The expression of Nvbrachyury around the presumptive border of the blastopore and Nvsnail genes in the presumptive endomesodermal gastrodermis of N. vectensis embryos occurs even before the morphological process of gastrulation begins (Scholz and Technau, 2003; Röttinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Components of the intracellular polarity Par system (NvaPKC, NvPar-6, NvPar-3, NvPar-1, and NvLgl) show a highly polarized bilaterian-like subcellular distribution throughout all epithelial cells at the blastula stage in N. vectensis.
source: Interestingly, the components of the intracellular polarity Par system (NvaPKC, NvPar-6, NvPar-3, NvPar-1, and NvLgl), which show a highly polarized bilaterian-like subcellular distribution throughout all epithelial cells at the blastula stage in N. vectensis (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015), are specifically degraded and down-regulated from the endomesoderm during the gastrulation process (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Par proteins are specifically degraded and down-regulated from the endomesoderm during the gastrulation process in N. vectensis.
source: Interestingly, the components of the intracellular polarity Par system (NvaPKC, NvPar-6, NvPar-3, NvPar-1, and NvLgl), which show a highly polarized bilaterian-like subcellular distribution throughout all epithelial cells at the blastula stage in N. vectensis (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015), are specifically degraded and down-regulated from the endomesoderm during the gastrulation process (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A showing the loss of Par proteins in the endomesoderm.

claim: Snail is necessary and sufficient to downregulate Par3 in Drosophila mesoderm, inducing the disassembly of junctional complexes in these tissues.
source: For example, it has been shown that snail is necessary and sufficient to downregulate Par3 in Drosophila mesoderm, inducing the disassembly of junctional complexes in these tissues (Weng and Wieschaus, 2016, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila.

claim: Nvbrachyury regulates epithelial apicobasal polarity of N. vectensis embryos.
source: In addition, we have shown that Nvbrachyury regulates epithelial apicobasal polarity of N. vectensis embryos, suggesting some aspects of epithelial cell polarity are highly conserved (Servetnick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: ß-catenin is not detectable in endomesodermal cells of either the gastrodermis or the pharynx at polyp stages in N. vectensis.
source: At polyp stages, neither ß-catenin (an AJ-associated protein) (Figure 1B and C) nor the Par proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) are detectable in endomesodermal cells of either the gastrodermis or the pharynx.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Clear localization of ß-catenin can be seen in the cortex of ectodermally derived epithelial cells in N. vectensis embryos.
source: When N. vectensis embryos are stained with antibodies to ß-catenin (Figure 1) or if Nvß-catenin::GFP mRNA is expressed in uncleaved zygotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), clear localization of ß-catenin can be seen in the cortex of ectodermally derived epithelial cells (Figures 1B, C, D, G and I), but not in endomesodermal cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live imaging data shown in multiple figures.

claim: ß-catenin is not localized in endomesodermal cells in N. vectensis embryos.
source: When N. vectensis embryos are stained with antibodies to ß-catenin (Figure 1) or if Nvß-catenin::GFP mRNA is expressed in uncleaved zygotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), clear localization of ß-catenin can be seen in the cortex of ectodermally derived epithelial cells (Figures 1B, C, D, G and I), but not in endomesodermal cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live imaging data shown in multiple figures.

claim: In pharyngeal cells of N. vectensis, Nvß-catenin, NvPar-6, and NvPar-1 expression begins to disappear during gastrulation and is localized only in the most apical regions.
source: In pharyngeal cells that are located between the epidermis and gastrodermis, Nvß-catenin (Figure 1B and D), NvPar-6 (Figure 1E), and NvPar-1 (Figure 1F) expression begins to disappear, and is localized only in the most apical regions, indicating that AJs are being disassembled/degraded during the gastrulation process (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: AJs are being disassembled/degraded during the gastrulation process in N. vectensis.
source: In pharyngeal cells that are located between the epidermis and gastrodermis, Nvß-catenin (Figure 1B and D), NvPar-6 (Figure 1E), and NvPar-1 (Figure 1F) expression begins to disappear, and is localized only in the most apical regions, indicating that AJs are being disassembled/degraded during the gastrulation process (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed loss of AJ-associated proteins during gastrulation.

claim: During later planula stages, ß-catenin and the components of the Par system display scattered patterns in the cytoplasm of a small subset of endomesodermal cells in N. vectensis.
source: During later planula stages, ß-catenin and the components of the Par system display scattered patterns in the cytoplasm of a small subset of endomesodermal cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Cells that undergo gastrulation in N. vectensis lose their polarized ectodermal cell-cell adhesion complex and components of the Par system, including ß-catenin, are downregulated from endomesodermal tissues.
source: Regardless of this scattered expression, it is clear that cells that undergo gastrulation in N. vectensis lose their polarized ectodermal cell-cell adhesion complex and components of the Par system, including ß-catenin, are downregulated from endomesodermal tissues (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In bilaterians, the proper formation of an epithelial paracellular barrier depends on the establishment of adhesive complexes between adjacent cells.
source: In bilaterians, the proper formation of an epithelial paracellular barrier (essential for tissue homeostasis) depends on the establishment of adhesive complexes between adjacent cells (Higashi et al., 2016; Jonusaite et al., 2016), which are regulated by the aPKC/Par complex (Ohno et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in bilaterians.

claim: Adhesive complexes between adjacent cells are regulated by the aPKC/Par complex in bilaterians.
source: In bilaterians, the proper formation of an epithelial paracellular barrier (essential for tissue homeostasis) depends on the establishment of adhesive complexes between adjacent cells (Higashi et al., 2016; Jonusaite et al., 2016), which are regulated by the aPKC/Par complex (Ohno et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: When juvenile N. vectensis polyps are incubated in 10,000 MW fluorescent dextran for 5–10 min, fluorescent dextran solution moves into the gastric cavity and then spreads into the mesoglea through the gastrodermal epithelium.
source: When juvenile polyps are incubated in dextran for 5–10 min (Figure 2B), fluorescent dextran solution moves into the gastric cavity and then spreads into the mesoglea through the gastrodermal epithelium (Figure 2C) but does not enter the mesoglea through the outer ectodermally-derived epidermis (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Fluorescent dextran does not enter the mesoglea through the outer ectodermally-derived epidermis in N. vectensis polyps.
source: When juvenile polyps are incubated in dextran for 5–10 min (Figure 2B), fluorescent dextran solution moves into the gastric cavity and then spreads into the mesoglea through the gastrodermal epithelium (Figure 2C) but does not enter the mesoglea through the outer ectodermally-derived epidermis (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Cell-cell adhesion is differentially regulated between the epidermis and gastrodermis in N. vectensis.
source: These results suggest that cell-cell adhesion is differentially regulated between the epidermis and gastrodermis and the absence/disruption of AJs may compromise Septate Junctions (SJs) in the gastrodermis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential dye penetration observed between epidermis and gastrodermis.

claim: The absence/disruption of AJs may compromise Septate Junctions (SJs) in the gastrodermis of N. vectensis.
source: These results suggest that cell-cell adhesion is differentially regulated between the epidermis and gastrodermis and the absence/disruption of AJs may compromise Septate Junctions (SJs) in the gastrodermis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed dye penetration.

claim: In N. vectensis polyps expressing a dominant negative version of NvPar-3::mVenus (dnNvPar-3), dye penetrated between epithelial cells in both the gastrodermis and the outer epidermis.
source: However, in polyps expressing a dominant negative version of NvPar-3::mVenus (dnNvPar-3; microinjected into uncleaved eggs) dye penetrated between epithelial cells in both the gastrodermis and the outer epidermis (Figures 2D, F and G), demonstrating an ancestral role of the aPKC/Par complex in the maintenance of cell-cell adhesion and the paracellular boundary (SJs) of epithelial cells during animal development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye penetration assay data shown in Figure 2D, F, and G.

claim: The aPKC/Par complex has an ancestral role in the maintenance of cell-cell adhesion and the paracellular boundary (SJs) of epithelial cells during animal development.
source: However, in polyps expressing a dominant negative version of NvPar-3::mVenus (dnNvPar-3; microinjected into uncleaved eggs) dye penetrated between epithelial cells in both the gastrodermis and the outer epidermis (Figures 2D, F and G), demonstrating an ancestral role of the aPKC/Par complex in the maintenance of cell-cell adhesion and the paracellular boundary (SJs) of epithelial cells during animal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that disruption of the Par complex affects paracellular barriers in N. vectensis.

claim: Pharmacological treatment of N. vectensis embryos with an aPKC activity inhibitor blocks cytokinesis but not mitosis in cleaving embryos.
source: Pharmacological treatment of N. vectensis embryos with an aPKC activity inhibitor blocks cytokinesis but not mitosis in cleaving embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A dominant negative version of NvPar-1 (dnNvPar-1), that lacks its kinase domain, localizes only to the cortex of cell–cell contacts in N. vectensis embryos.
source: In addition, a dominant negative version of NvPar-1 (dnNvPar-1), that lacks its kinase domain, localizes only to the cortex of cell–cell contacts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NvPar-1 is phosphorylated by NvaPKC in N. vectensis.
source: Since NvPar-1 is phosphorylated by NvaPKC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we predict that, as in other systems, dnNvPar-1 could be phosphorylated by aPKC but would not phosphorylate the aPKC/Par complex (Vaccari et al., 2005; Böhm et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The formation of cell–cell contacts is regulated by the activity of the aPKC/Par complex in N. vectensis embryos.
source: These results together suggest that the formation of cell–cell contacts is regulated by the activity of the aPKC/Par complex in N. vectensis embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results with aPKC inhibitor and dnNvPar-1.

claim: When NvPar-6 and NvPar-3 are mutated by CRISPR/Cas9, the ectodermal epithelium loses its integrity, presenting changes in thickness.
source: When NvPar-6 and NvPar-3 are mutated, the ectodermal epithelium loses its integrity, presenting changes in thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and interestingly, the endomesoderm (which does not express these proteins) generates cells with mesenchymal-like morphotypes that are never normally seen in this species (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In Nvpar-6 and Nvpar-3 mutant embryos, the endomesoderm generates cells with mesenchymal-like morphotypes that are never normally seen in N. vectensis.
source: When NvPar-6 and NvPar-3 are mutated, the ectodermal epithelium loses its integrity, presenting changes in thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and interestingly, the endomesoderm (which does not express these proteins) generates cells with mesenchymal-like morphotypes that are never normally seen in this species (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: In Nvpar-6 and Nvpar-3 mutant embryos, there is disruption of microtubules and actin cytoskeleton.
source: In Nvpar-6 and Nvpar-3 mutant embryos, we also observed the disruption of microtubules and actin cytoskeleton (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), and AJs (visualized with the ß-catenin antibody in Figure 4) that confirms our previous observations of their role in regulating ectodermal cell polarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: In Nvpar-6 and Nvpar-3 mutant embryos, there is disruption of AJs.
source: In Nvpar-6 and Nvpar-3 mutant embryos, we also observed the disruption of microtubules and actin cytoskeleton (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), and AJs (visualized with the ß-catenin antibody in Figure 4) that confirms our previous observations of their role in regulating ectodermal cell polarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The primary defect in NvPar3 KO embryos is in aspects of cell adhesion and not cell type specification.
source: Although it was difficult to dissect significant changes in the expression of germ layer markers (e.g. Nvbra, Nvsnail, NvSix3/6, and Nvfz10) from the morphological changes associated with epithelial integrity when these genes were disrupted (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E), it is clear that the primary defect in NvPar3 KO were aspects of cell adhesion and not cell type specification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that germ layer markers are still expressed despite morphological defects in NvPar3 KO embryos.

claim: Only ectodermal- but not endomesodermal-lineages are affected by NvPar-3 mutations in single blastomere injection experiments.
source: Our results show that only ectodermal- but not endomesodermal-lineages are affected by these mutations (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single blastomere injection CRISPR/Cas9 data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Presumptive ectodermal cells derived from an injected blastomere fail to maintain AJs and the resulting clone of epithelial cells loses its structural integrity inducing cell extrusion.
source: Presumptive ectodermal cells derived from an injected blastomere fail to maintain AJs (and potentially SJs) and the resulting clone of epithelial cells loses its structural integrity inducing cell extrusion.
evidence: This is a description of the observed phenotype in single blastomere injection experiments.

claim: Presumptive endomesodermal cells derived from an injected blastomere develop into a normal endomesodermal epithelium.
source: In contrast, presumptive endomesodermal cells derived from an injected blastomere develop into a normal endomesodermal epithelium (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The proper cell-cell adhesion of the ectodermal layer regulates trans-epithelially the integrity of the endomesodermal layer in N. vectensis.
source: Our results complement the work of (Kirillova et al., 2018) and demonstrate that the proper cell-cell adhesion of the ectodermal layer somehow regulates trans-epithelially the integrity of the endomesodermal layer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting ectodermal Par proteins affects endomesodermal integrity.

claim: In bilaterians, AJs recruit members of the aPKC/Par complex and the direct interaction between Par-3 and aPKC/Par-6 is required for the maintenance and maturation of AJs.
source: In bilaterians, AJs recruit members of the aPKC/Par complex and the direct interaction between Par-3 and aPKC/Par-6 is required for the maintenance and maturation of AJs (Ohno et al., 2015; Ragkousi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in bilaterians.

claim: Cortical co-localization of NvPar-3 and Nvß-catenin is observed at the cell boundaries in the ectodermal epithelium of embryos co-injected with NvPar-3::mVenus and Nvß-catenin::RFP.
source: We observed cortical co-localization of NvPar-3 and Nvß-catenin at the cell boundaries in the ectodermal epithelium of embryos co-injected with NvPar-3::mVenus and Nvß-catenin::RFP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In embryos co-injected with Nvß-catenin::RFP and dnNvPar-3::mVenus, there is an alteration of the sub-cellular expression of Nvß-catenin::RFP in all cells due to the translocation of ß-catenin from the cortical AJs into cell nuclei.
source: However, in embryos co-injected with Nvß-catenin::RFP and dnNvPar-3::mVenus, we observed an alteration of the sub-cellular expression of Nvß-catenin::RFP in all cells due to the translocation of ß-catenin from the cortical AJs into cell nuclei (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of N. vectensis embryos with 5 µm 1-azakenpaullone (AZ; an inhibitor of GSK-3ß and a canonical Wnt agonist) results in an expansion of the expression domain of Par-6 and a stabilization of AJs in endomesodermal cells.
source: In addition, results from N. vectensis embryos treated with 5 µm 1-azakenpaullone (AZ; an inhibitor of GSK-3ß and a canonical Wnt agonist) suggest that GSK-3ß stabilizes AJs of epithelial cells in N. vectensis embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We observed an expansion of the expression domain of Par-6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and a stabilization of AJs (labeled with ß-catenin in Figure 5—figure supplement 1) in endomesodermal cells of treated embryos, which was never observed in control embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by the drug treatment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GSK-3ß stabilizes AJs of epithelial cells in N. vectensis embryos.
source: In addition, results from N. vectensis embryos treated with 5 µm 1-azakenpaullone (AZ; an inhibitor of GSK-3ß and a canonical Wnt agonist) suggest that GSK-3ß stabilizes AJs of epithelial cells in N. vectensis embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that inhibiting GSK-3ß leads to AJ stabilization.

claim: NvPar-3 recruits Nvß-catenin protein and stabilizes its localization at the apico-lateral cortex of ectodermal cells through the formation of AJs.
source: Here, we show in vivo embryonic evidence suggesting that NvPar-3 (whose cortical localization is normally inhibited by Par-1) recruits Nvß-catenin protein and stabilizes its localization at the apico-lateral cortex of ectodermal cells through the formation of AJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-localization and functional experiments with NvPar-3 and Nvß-catenin.

claim: The putative disassembly of the aPKC/Par complex induced by dnNvPar-3 overexpression induces the nuclearization of Nvß-catenin protein due to its cytosolic availability caused by AJs disruption.
source: Furthermore, the putative disassembly of the aPKC/Par complex induced by dnNvPar-3 overexpression, induces the nuclearization of Nvß-catenin protein (Figure 5A) due to its cytosolic availability caused by AJs disruption.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed nuclear localization of ß-catenin when dnNvPar-3 is overexpressed.

claim: Extrusion of individual cells from the ectodermal epithelium is observed in dnNvPar-3 treated-embryos and single injected-blastomere CRISPR/Cas9 NvPar-3 knock-out.
source: Strikingly, we also observed the extrusion of individual cells from the ectodermal epithelium of dnNvPar-3 treated-embryos (Figure 5C) and single injected-blastomere CRISPR/Cas9 NvPar-3 knock-out (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Treatments with dnNvPar-3 induce EMT-like processes in N. vectensis embryos.
source: This suggests that these treatments induce EMT-like processes, not observed under control conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed cell extrusion phenotype.

claim: N. vectensis has two snail genes, Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B, which are both expressed in the endomesodermal plate prior to and throughout the gastrulation process.
source: N. vectensis has two snail genes, Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B, which are both expressed in the endomesodermal plate prior to and throughout the gastrulation process, and which define the boundary between gastrodermis and ectodermal pharynx (Magie et al., 2007; Röttinger et al., 2012; Amiel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The overexpression of both NvSnail-A::mCherry and NvSnail-B::mCherry together induces the ectopic translocation of Nvß-catenin::GFP to the nuclei of ectodermal cells.
source: The overexpression of both proteins NvSnail-A::mCherry and NvSnail-B::mCherry together induce the ectopic translocation of Nvß-catenin::GFP to the nuclei of ectodermal cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of both NvSnail::mCherry proteins delocalizes NvPar-3 from the cell cortex when co-expressed with NvPar-3::mVenus.
source: This treatment also delocalizes NvPar-3 from the cell cortex when both NvSnail::mCherry proteins are co-expressed with NvPar-3::mVenus (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression of Nvsnail genes is sufficient to induce the degradation of Par proteins and AJs from the ectoderm and disrupts its epithelial integrity.
source: Similar to the Nvpar-3 knock-out (Figure 4), the expression of Nvsnail genes is sufficient to induce the degradation of Par proteins and AJs (ß-catenin) from the ectoderm and disrupts its epithelial integrity; however, nuclear ß-catenin was not observed under these treatments (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the single blastomere injection data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Nuclear Nvß-catenin::GFP observed in vivo when NvSnail proteins are overexpressed is a consequence of the high cytosolic availability generated by its ectopic overexpression and release from AJs.
source: Thus, nuclear Nvß-catenin::GFP observed in vivo when we overexpressed NvSnail proteins (Figure 6A) is a consequence of the high cytosolic availability generated by its ectopic overexpression and release from AJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Not every ectodermal cell is affected by Nvsnail overexpression even though all of the cells express the injected mRNAs.
source: Interestingly, not every ectodermal cell was affected by these treatments even though all of the cells expressed the injected mRNAs (Figure 6A and E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 6A, E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The response to Nvsnail over-expression is spatially regulated.
source: This patched pattern suggests that the response to Nvsnail over-expression is spatially regulated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the patched pattern of affected cells.

claim: The role of Nvsnail genes on AJs and apicobasal cell polarity is constrained to the site of gastrulation in N. vectensis embryos under natural conditions.
source: These results suggest that the role of Nvsnail genes on AJs and apicobasal cell polarity is constrained to the site of gastrulation in N. vectensis embryos under natural conditions, and that these genes may be required for gastrulation movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial regulation of Nvsnail effects.

claim: Snail genes temporally down-regulate E-cadherin during mesoderm segregation and EMT in bilaterian animals.
source: The snail genes temporally down-regulate E-cadherin during mesoderm segregation and EMT in bilaterian animals (Lim and Thiery, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The cells comprising the endomesodermal plate lose their cell-cell adhesion during gastrulation in N. vectensis embryos.
source: As we have shown here, as well as in previous studies (Magie et al., 2007; Magie and Martindale, 2008), the cells comprising the endomesodermal plate lose their cell-cell adhesion during gastrulation in N. vectensis embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study and previous citations.

claim: Once gastrulation is complete and the pharynx forms, components of the Par system and the ß-catenin components of the AJs are degraded from both the cortex and cytoplasm of endomesodermal cells.
source: Our data suggest that once gastrulation is complete and the pharynx forms, components of the Par system and the ß-catenin components of the AJs are degraded from both the cortex and cytoplasm of endomesodermal cells (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In CRISPR/Cas9 mutants for Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B, the endomesodermal plate forms but it does not migrate further than its first invagination during gastrulation.
source: In CRISPR/Cas9 mutants, the endomesodermal plate forms but it does not migrate further than its first invagination during gastrulation (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPR/Cas9 knockout data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In CRISPR/Cas9 mutants for Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B, AJs and apical Par proteins are retained at the apical cortex of the cells of the endomesodermal plate.
source: Furthermore, AJs (labeled with ß-catenin) and apical Par proteins (labeled with antiNvPar-6 and antiNvaPKC) are retained at the apical cortex of the cells of the endomesodermal plate (Figure 7B and C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B, C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: NvPar-1 and NvLgl were not detected in endomesodermal cells of Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B CRISPR/Cas9 mutants.
source: Surprisingly, NvPar-1 and NvLgl were not detected in those cells (Figure 7C), suggesting that the degradation of these basolateral proteins precede or do not depend on the activity of the Nvsnail genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The degradation of NvPar-1 and NvLgl precedes or does not depend on the activity of the Nvsnail genes.
source: Surprisingly, NvPar-1 and NvLgl were not detected in those cells (Figure 7C), suggesting that the degradation of these basolateral proteins precede or do not depend on the activity of the Nvsnail genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NvPar-1 and NvLgl are absent even when Nvsnail is knocked out.

claim: Nvsnail regulates apical cell-polarity, AJs turnover, and the migration ('zippering') but not the invagination of the endomesodermal plate during gastrulation of N. vectensis embryos.
source: This suggests that Nvsnail regulates apical cell-polarity, AJs turnover, and the migration ('zippering') but not the invagination of the endomesodermal plate during gastrulation of N. vectensis embryos (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Nvsnail knockout phenotype.

claim: The invagination of the endomesodermal plate (controlled by the Wnt/PCP pathway) is uncoupled from its specification in N. vectensis embryos.
source: Interestingly, the invagination of the endomesodermal plate (controlled by the Wnt/PCP pathway) is uncoupled from its specification in N. vectensis embryos (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wijesena et al., 2011), which is consistent with our observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is consistent with the current observations.

claim: By disrupting the aPKC/Par complex in N. vectensis, cells from the endomesodermal epithelium can be converted into mesenchymal-like cells.
source: We have shown that by disrupting the aPKC/Par complex (apicobasal cell-polarity) in N. vectensis (Figures 3, 4 and 5), we are able to convert cells from the endomesodermal epithelium into mesenchymal-like cells, translocate Nvß-catenin (Figure 5A), and emulate EMT-like processes (apical constriction and individual cell-detachments) in the ectodermal epithelium of N. vectensis treated-embryos (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The cnidarian N. vectensis possesses mechanisms necessary to segregate individual germ layers (e.g. mesoderm and NCC) described in bilaterians; however, they do not do it.
source: These results demonstrate that the cnidarian N. vectensis possesses mechanisms necessary to segregate individual germ layers (e.g. mesoderm and NCC) described in bilaterians; however, they do not do it.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that N. vectensis can undergo EMT-like processes when Par proteins are disrupted.

claim: The N. vectensis embryo is composed of two independent morphogenetic modules that are integrated and organized by the pharynx.
source: Our working hypothesis is that the N. vectensis embryo is composed of two independent morphogenetic modules that are integrated and organized by the pharynx (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The ectoderm, whose apicobasal polarity is regulated by Nvbrachyury, promotes ectodermal epithelial morphogenesis and pharynx formation.
source: The first observation is that the ectoderm, whose apicobasal polarity (and thus, AJs and epithelial integrity) is regulated by Nvbrachyury that promotes ectodermal epithelial morphogenesis and pharynx formation (Servetnick et al., 2017), and the second module is generated by endomesodermal differentiation and cell-movements that are regulated by Nvsnail genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Endomesodermal differentiation and cell-movements are regulated by Nvsnail genes.
source: The first observation is that the ectoderm, whose apicobasal polarity (and thus, AJs and epithelial integrity) is regulated by Nvbrachyury that promotes ectodermal epithelial morphogenesis and pharynx formation (Servetnick et al., 2017), and the second module is generated by endomesodermal differentiation and cell-movements that are regulated by Nvsnail genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results with Nvsnail knockouts.

claim: Both morphogenetic modules in N. vectensis are specified by nuclear ß-catenin (maternal).
source: Additional work is required to elucidate any differences in function between Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B genes, however, both modules are specified by nuclear ß-catenin (Röttinger et al., 2012), suggesting that the nuclear ß-catenin (maternal) shift from the animal pole in cnidarians to the vegetal pole in bilaterians is mechanistically plausible and sufficient to re-specify the site of gastrulation and germ-layers along the animal-vegetal axis during Metazoan evolution (Martindale and Lee, 2013; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The nuclear ß-catenin (maternal) shift from the animal pole in cnidarians to the vegetal pole in bilaterians is mechanistically plausible and sufficient to re-specify the site of gastrulation and germ-layers along the animal-vegetal axis during Metazoan evolution.
source: Additional work is required to elucidate any differences in function between Nvsnail-A and Nvsnail-B genes, however, both modules are specified by nuclear ß-catenin (Röttinger et al., 2012), suggesting that the nuclear ß-catenin (maternal) shift from the animal pole in cnidarians to the vegetal pole in bilaterians is mechanistically plausible and sufficient to re-specify the site of gastrulation and germ-layers along the animal-vegetal axis during Metazoan evolution (Martindale and Lee, 2013; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current findings and cited work.

claim: During NCC migration, cells display 'partial-EMT' where cells remain attached to several neighboring cells but their apicobasal polarity and AJs are down-regulated, allowing collective-cell migration.
source: For example, during NCC migration, cells display 'partial-EMT' where cells remain attached to several neighboring cells but their apicobasal polarity and AJs are down-regulated, allowing collective-cell migration (Weng and Wieschaus, 2017; Nieto et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2006; Theveneau and Mayor, 2013; Ribeiro and Paredes, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 'Partial-EMT' may be the mechanism by which the endomesodermal epithelium migrates into the blastocoel in N. vectensis embryos during normal gastrulation.
source: Our data suggest that 'partial-EMT' may be the mechanism by which the endomesodermal epithelium migrates into the blastocoel in N. vectensis embryos during normal gastrulation (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the authors' data.

claim: N. vectensis has both up and downstream cellular and molecular mechanisms associated with EMT described in bilaterians.
source: In conclusion, N. vectensis has both up and downstream cellular and molecular mechanisms associated with EMT described in bilaterians.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: N. vectensis does not segregate a distinct mesodermal germ layer nor display EMT under natural conditions.
source: However, N. vectensis does not segregate a distinct mesodermal germ layer nor display EMT under natural conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of observed fact.

claim: In bilaterians, the mechanism to segregate mesodermal cells from the endoderm must have evolved to retain the tight cell-cell junctions required in endodermal epithelia.
source: In bilaterians, this mechanism must have evolved to segregate mesodermal cells from the endoderm to retain the tight cell-cell junctions required in endodermal epithelia.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: In Drosophila embryos, contractile myosin enhances the localization of AJs and Par-3 in the presumptive mesoderm and prevents their downregulation by Snail, thus delaying EMT.
source: Interestingly, mesoderm segregation via EMT in Drosophila takes place after epithelial folding in response to snail expression. In these embryos, contractile myosin enhances the localization of AJs and Par-3 in the presumptive mesoderm and prevents their downregulation by Snail, thus delaying EMT (Weng and Wieschaus, 2016, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The overexpression of Snail in Drosophila embryos is sufficient to disassemble ectodermal-AJs, but mesodermal-AJs are maintained by actomyosin contraction that antagonize Snail effects.
source: Furthermore, the overexpression of Snail in Drosophila embryos is sufficient to disassemble ectodermal-AJs, but mesodermal-AJs are maintained by actomyosin contraction that antagonize Snail effects (Weng and Wieschaus, 2016, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Nvsnail overexpression in endomesodermal lineages is not sufficient to segregate cells and the endomesoderm remains as an epithelium in N. vectensis.
source: Our results suggest a similar mechanism since Nvsnail overexpression in endomesodermal lineages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is not sufficient to segregate cells and the endomesoderm remains as an epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unlike Drosophila, Par proteins and AJs are not enhanced but degraded during the gastrulation of N. vectensis.
source: However, unlike Drosophila, Par proteins and AJs are not enhanced but degraded during the gastrulation of N. vectensis (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Not only the degradation but also the turnover of AJs and Par proteins in adjacent epithelia is essential for EMT-mediated germ layer segregation in different animals.
source: As it is discussed in (Weng and Wieschaus, 2017), not only the degradation but also the turnover of AJs and Par proteins in adjacent epithelia is essential for EMT-mediated germ layer segregation in different animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The dual identity of N. vectensis endomesoderm is characterized by the continuous expression of Nvsnail genes that repress the turnover of AJs and may play a role in inhibiting EMT from occurring.
source: The dual identity of N. vectensis endomesoderm is characterized by the continuous expression of Nvsnail genes (Martindale et al., 2004) that repress the turnover of AJs and may play a role in inhibiting EMT from occurring (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited work.

claim: Components of the Wnt/PCP pathway are expressed only in the endomesoderm of N. vectensis.
source: Interestingly, components of the Wnt/PCP pathway are expressed only in the endomesoderm (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wijesena et al., 2011), while components of the Par system are expressed only in the ectoderm (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Components of the Par system are expressed only in the ectoderm of N. vectensis.
source: Interestingly, components of the Wnt/PCP pathway are expressed only in the endomesoderm (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wijesena et al., 2011), while components of the Par system are expressed only in the ectoderm (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: NvSnail degrades AJs and inhibits their re-assembly in the endomesoderm, but the activation of contractile myosin by the Wnt/PCP pathway maintains the endomesodermal cells together in N. vectensis embryos.
source: It could be that NvSnail degrades AJs and inhibits their re-assembly in the endomesoderm, but the activation of contractile myosin by the Wnt/PCP pathway maintains the endomesodermal cells together in N. vectensis embryos.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: In bilaterians, a mechanism (most likely downstream of Snail) that connects the cytoskeleton with cell-polarity may have evolved to tighten cell-cell adhesion in the endoderm and allow EMT.
source: Hence in bilaterians, a mechanism (most likely downstream of Snail) that connects the cytoskeleton with cell-polarity may have evolved to tighten cell-cell adhesion in the endoderm and allow EMT.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Different modes of gastrulation have been described between cnidarian species including unipolar and multipolar cell ingression and delamination.
source: In cnidarians, different modes of gastrulation have been described between species including unipolar and multipolar cell ingression and delamination (Kirillova et al., 2018; Byrum and Martindale, 2004; Marlow and Martindale, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Poriferans display EMT-like processes and cell morphologies during regeneration and trans-differentiation.
source: Poriferans display EMT-like processes and cell morphologies during regeneration and trans-differentiation (Nakanishi et al., 2014; Coutinho et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Ctenophores segregate a mesodermal cell population during embryogenesis but do not have the genes that encode for all cell-cell adhesion complexes and specify for mesoderm in bilaterians.
source: Interestingly, ctenophores segregate a mesodermal cell population during embryogenesis but do not have the genes that encode for all cell-cell adhesion complexes and specify for mesoderm in bilaterians (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) (Ganot et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1.
